en.title: Business Administration: The Whole Course
en.short: What business administration is, how degrees are organised, and how to study its main areas.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Business administration is the study of how organisations are planned, run and improved. It asks how people, money, materials and information can be combined to reach a goal. That goal may be profit, as in a company. It may also be a service, as in a hospital, a charity or a government agency.

The field draws on other subjects. Economics explains markets. Psychology and sociology explain people at work. Mathematics and statistics support decisions. Law sets the rules. A manager needs some knowledge of each, and needs to see how they connect. A price change, for example, affects sales, cash, staff workload and stock levels at the same time.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and by institution. A BSc or BBA often takes three or four years. In Nigeria, the National Universities Commission sets minimum standards for universities, and the National Board for Technical Education does the same for polytechnics. A polytechnic student there usually takes the ND and then, after a period of industrial experience, the HND. In Ghana, the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission regulates this level of education. Kenya and South Africa have their own regulators and national qualification frameworks.

Early years usually teach foundations. Later years add specialist courses, such as finance, marketing or human resources, and often a project. An MBA is a master’s degree, and many programmes expect work experience. It covers the same functions at speed, then focuses on strategy, leadership and research.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
First come the business environment, basic economics, management principles, organisational structure and organisational behaviour. Students also meet marketing, financial accounting, descriptive statistics and entrepreneurship.

The next stage goes deeper into each function. Human resource management deals with hiring, developing and rewarding people. Marketing moves on to strategy, pricing and digital channels. Management accounting supports internal decisions. Corporate finance deals with investment choices and funding. Operations and supply chain management deal with making and delivering goods and services. Business law and ethics set the limits of acceptable conduct. Inferential statistics supports decisions based on samples. Strategic management, international business and information systems then bring the functions together.

At master’s level, students study corporate strategy, which asks what businesses a group should own. They also study leadership and organisational change, and research methods for the dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn each model by asking three questions. What problem does it solve? What information does it need? Where does it fail? Examiners reward students who can apply a model to a case, not students who only describe it.

Practise calculations by hand until you can explain every step. State the meaning of each answer, such as whether a project should go ahead. Read business news, annual reports and company websites, and connect them to your course. Check any fact about a named company against a reliable source, because companies change quickly. For law, tax and accounting standards, always check the current official source for your country. The material in these summaries is for learning and is not professional advice.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students list theories without linking them to the question. Others treat a model as a fact. Maslow’s hierarchy, for example, is a useful idea, but the research support for it is limited.

Other common errors are mixing up profit and cash, mark-up and margin, or correlation and causation. Some students present one country’s law as if it applied everywhere. Others give a final number with no units and no recommendation. In case studies, some repeat the case facts and offer no analysis. Finally, avoid vague advice such as saying a firm should improve its marketing. Say what it should do, why, what it would cost and how success would be measured.

keyPoints: Business administration studies how people, money, materials and information are combined to reach a goal.
Degrees start with foundations, then go deeper into each function, then bring the functions together in strategy.
Learn each model by asking what problem it solves, what information it needs and where it fails.
Apply models to the case, and end with a clear, costed recommendation.
Laws, tax rules and standards differ by country, so check the current official source for yours.

en.title: Business, Its Forms and Its Environment
en.short: What a business is, the main legal forms, stakeholders, and how PESTEL describes the environment.

sections.heading: Legal forms of business
sections.text:
A business is an organisation that provides goods or services, usually to earn a profit. Its legal form decides who owns it, who carries the risk and how it is taxed.

A sole trader is one person who owns and runs the business. It is simple to start, but in general the owner is personally liable for all debts. A partnership has two or more owners who share profit and, in a general partnership, liability. A company is a separate legal person. Its members usually have limited liability, which means they can lose only what they invested or agreed to invest. A private company cannot offer its shares to the public. A public company can, and may list on a stock exchange. Co-operatives are owned by their members, and state enterprises by government.

The details differ by country. Nigeria’s Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, for example, allows one person to form a private company and provides for limited liability partnerships.

sections.heading: Stakeholders
sections.text: A stakeholder is any person or group that affects, or is affected by, a business. Internal stakeholders include employees and managers. External stakeholders include customers, suppliers, lenders, communities and government. Their interests can conflict. Customers want low prices, while employees want higher pay.

sections.heading: Reading the environment with PESTEL
sections.text:
The external environment is everything outside the firm that can affect it. PESTEL is a checklist for scanning it: political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors.

Consider a made-up cassava flour firm in Ghana. A new export rule is a legal factor. A weaker cedi is an economic factor, and it can make imported packaging cost more. Growing demand for gluten-free food is a social factor. Solar drying is a technological factor. PESTEL only collects facts. The useful step is to decide which factors matter most, and what the firm should do about them.

keyPoints: Legal form decides ownership, liability and tax treatment.
A company is a legal person separate from its members.
Limited liability restricts a member’s loss to what was invested or promised.
Stakeholder interests can conflict, so managers must balance them.
PESTEL is a scanning tool, and its value lies in the conclusions you draw.

en.title: Economics for Business
en.short: Scarcity, demand and supply, costs, market structures and the main measures of the whole economy.

sections.heading: Scarcity, demand and supply
sections.text:
Economics studies how people and firms choose when resources are scarce. Every choice has an opportunity cost, which is the value of the best option given up. Microeconomics looks at single markets and firms. Macroeconomics looks at the whole economy.

Demand is the quantity buyers will purchase at each price. Supply is the quantity sellers will offer at each price. A market tends toward the equilibrium price, where the two are equal. Take a made-up rice market in Kano, with P in thousands of naira per bag. Demand is Qd = 500 − 2P and supply is Qs = 100 + 2P.
500 − 2P = 100 + 2P
400 = 4P, so P = 100, which is ₦100,000 a bag
Quantity = 500 − 2 × 100 = 300 bags

sections.heading: Costs and market structure
sections.text:
Economies of scale mean that average cost falls as output grows. Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, and marginal revenue is the income from it. In standard theory, a firm earns the most profit where the two are equal.

Market structure shapes pricing power. Perfect competition has many firms selling identical products, so each accepts the market price. Monopolistic competition has many firms with differentiated products. Oligopoly has a few large firms that watch each other. Monopoly has one main seller.

sections.heading: The whole economy
sections.text:
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period. Inflation is a general rise in prices, often measured with a consumer price index. Suppose a made-up index rises from 200 to 230 in a year.
Inflation = (230 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%

Central banks usually influence demand through interest rates, which is monetary policy. Governments use taxes and spending, which is fiscal policy. A weaker currency makes imports more expensive and can help exporters. Managers watch these measures when they set prices and plan borrowing and stock.

keyPoints: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option given up.
The equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
In standard theory, profit is greatest where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
The four main market structures are perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly.
GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced in a period.
Inflation rate = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100.

en.title: Principles of Management
en.short: The functions of management, the classical and human relations schools, and managers’ roles and skills.

sections.heading: What managers do
sections.text:
Management is the work of reaching goals through other people and through resources. Modern textbooks usually name four functions. Planning sets goals and decides how to reach them. Organising arranges people and tasks. Leading motivates and directs people. Controlling compares results with the plan and corrects any gaps.

A good manager is both effective and efficient. Effectiveness means reaching the right goal. Efficiency means using few resources to reach it.

sections.heading: How management thought developed
sections.text:
Frederick Taylor published The Principles of Scientific Management in 1911. He studied tasks closely to find the most efficient method, then trained workers in it and paid by output. Critics say this treats people like machines.

Henri Fayol, a French mining executive, looked at the whole organisation. He described five management activities and fourteen principles, including division of work and unity of command. Max Weber described bureaucracy, which relies on written rules, a clear hierarchy and appointment by merit.

The Hawthorne studies at Western Electric in the USA, in the 1920s and 1930s, drew attention to social factors at work. They led to the human relations school. Scholars still debate how the results should be read. Later, systems theory saw the organisation as parts that depend on each other. Contingency theory argued that the best method depends on the situation.

sections.heading: Roles and skills
sections.text:
Henry Mintzberg observed managers at work and described ten roles in three groups: interpersonal, informational and decisional. Robert Katz named three skills: technical, human and conceptual. Technical skill matters most for first-line supervisors. Conceptual skill, which is the ability to see the whole organisation, matters most for top managers. Human skill matters at every level.

Imagine Wanjiru, the made-up manager of a Nairobi bakery. She sets a monthly sales target, which is planning. She draws up shifts, which is organising. She encourages a tired team, which is leading. She checks waste each week, which is controlling.

keyPoints: The four usual functions are planning, organising, leading and controlling.
Effectiveness is reaching the right goal, and efficiency is using few resources.
Taylor focused on tasks, Fayol on the whole organisation, and Weber on bureaucracy.
The Hawthorne studies drew attention to social factors at work.
Contingency theory says no single method suits every situation.
Katz’s three skills are technical, human and conceptual.

en.title: Organisational Structure and Design
en.short: How work is divided and coordinated, with functional, divisional and matrix structures compared.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.text:
Organisational structure is the formal pattern of jobs and reporting lines. An organisation chart, also called an organogram, shows it. Designers make several choices.

Division of work decides how tasks are split into jobs. Departmentalisation groups those jobs. The chain of command shows who reports to whom. Span of control is the number of people who report to one manager. A wide span gives a flat structure with few levels. A narrow span gives a tall structure with more levels.

Centralisation means that top managers keep most decisions. Decentralisation moves decisions to lower levels, closer to customers. Delegation means giving someone the authority to do a task. The manager remains accountable for the result.

sections.heading: Common structures
sections.text:
A functional structure groups staff by specialism, such as finance or marketing. It builds expertise and suits a firm with one main product. Departments may fail to work together, however.

A divisional structure groups staff by product, region or customer. A made-up bank might have divisions for Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya. Each division can respond to its own market, but some functions may be duplicated.

A matrix structure combines the two, so an employee reports to both a functional manager and a project manager. It shares skills across projects. The two bosses can cause conflict and confusion. Network structures outsource many activities to partner firms.

sections.heading: Choosing a structure
sections.text:
No structure is best in every case. Tom Burns and G. M. Stalker, studying firms in the UK, separated mechanistic and organic organisations. Mechanistic organisations have clear rules and strict hierarchy, and they suit stable conditions. Organic organisations are flexible and rely on shared knowledge, and they suit fast change.

Size, strategy, technology and environment all influence the choice. A small firm is often run directly by its owner. As it grows, the owner can no longer make every decision, and a more formal structure usually becomes necessary.

keyPoints: Structure is the formal pattern of jobs and reporting lines.
A wide span of control produces a flatter organisation.
Delegation passes authority, but the manager remains accountable.
Functional structures build expertise, and divisional structures focus on markets.
A matrix gives an employee two bosses, which can cause conflict.
Mechanistic designs suit stability, and organic designs suit change.

en.title: Organisational Behaviour: Motivation, Teams and Culture
en.short: Why people act as they do at work: personality, motivation theories, team development and culture.

sections.heading: Individuals and motivation
sections.text:
Organisational behaviour studies how individuals and groups act at work. Personality is one influence. The Big Five model describes openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Research links conscientiousness with job performance in many kinds of work.

Motivation is the force that directs effort. Content theories ask what people need. Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy from physiological needs to self-actualisation. Evidence for a strict order is weak. Frederick Herzberg separated hygiene factors, such as pay and conditions, from motivators, such as achievement and responsibility. Poor hygiene factors cause dissatisfaction, but improving them may not motivate on its own.

Process theories ask how people decide. Victor Vroom’s expectancy theory says effort depends on three beliefs: effort will lead to performance, performance will lead to a reward, and the reward is valued. J. Stacy Adams’s equity theory says people compare their rewards with those of others. Goal-setting theory, from Edwin Locke, finds that specific, difficult goals often raise performance more than vague ones.

sections.heading: Teams
sections.text: Bruce Tuckman described stages of group development: forming, storming, norming and performing. A later stage, adjourning, was added for when a team ends. Real teams may not follow this order exactly. Social loafing happens when individuals make less effort in a group. Clear individual roles can reduce it.

sections.heading: Culture
sections.text:
Organisational culture is the set of shared values and assumptions that guide behaviour. Edgar Schein described three levels: visible artefacts, stated values and deep basic assumptions. Culture is hard to change, because the deepest level is rarely discussed.

Take a made-up case. Thabo’s call centre in Durban raises pay, yet staff turnover stays high. Staff say their work is dull and that nobody listens to them. Herzberg’s theory suggests that pay was not the main problem. Job redesign and giving staff a voice may help more.

keyPoints: Content theories ask what people need, and process theories ask how they decide.
Herzberg separates hygiene factors from motivators.
Expectancy theory rests on effort, performance and valued reward.
Tuckman’s stages are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
Schein’s levels of culture are artefacts, values and basic assumptions.
Maslow’s hierarchy is well known, but evidence for its strict order is weak.

en.title: Marketing Fundamentals
en.short: Customer needs, segmentation, targeting, positioning, the marketing mix and the product life cycle.

sections.heading: What marketing is
sections.text:
Marketing is the process of understanding what customers need, then creating and delivering value that meets that need at a profit. It is much wider than advertising. It starts with research and continues after the sale.

Market research collects information. Primary data is new data that you collect yourself, for example through a survey. Secondary data already exists, for example in a census or an industry report. Buyers usually pass through five stages: recognising a need, searching for information, comparing options, buying, and evaluating after the purchase.

sections.heading: Segmentation, targeting and positioning
sections.text:
A market is rarely one uniform group. Segmentation divides it into groups with similar needs, using factors such as age, location, income, lifestyle or usage. Targeting chooses the groups to serve. Positioning decides how the product should be seen in the minds of those buyers, compared with its rivals.

Consider a made-up yoghurt brand in Accra. It might target busy office workers, and position itself as a healthy, quick breakfast.

sections.heading: The marketing mix
sections.text: The marketing mix is the set of tools a firm controls. E. Jerome McCarthy’s four Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Place means how the product reaches buyers. Services often add three more Ps, from Bernard Booms and Mary Bitner: people, process and physical evidence. Physical evidence means what customers can see, such as a clean branch or a printed receipt. All parts must fit together. A premium price with a cheap-looking package sends a confused message.

sections.heading: The product life cycle
sections.text: The product life cycle describes four stages of sales over time. In the introduction stage, sales are low and costs are high. In growth, sales rise quickly and rivals enter. In maturity, sales level off and competition on price increases. In decline, sales fall, and the firm may update or withdraw the product. The stages are a guide and not a law. Their length varies widely, and marketing decisions can themselves change the shape of the curve.

keyPoints: Marketing begins with customer needs, and it is more than advertising.
STP stands for segmentation, targeting and positioning.
The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.
Services often add people, process and physical evidence.
Primary data is new, and secondary data already exists.
The life cycle stages are introduction, growth, maturity and decline.

en.title: Financial Accounting Basics
en.short: The accounting equation, double entry, accruals and depreciation, with a worked example.

sections.heading: The accounting equation
sections.text:
Financial accounting records a firm’s transactions and reports them to outsiders, such as investors and lenders. Its base is the accounting equation: assets = liabilities + equity. Assets are resources the firm controls. Liabilities are amounts it owes. Equity is the owners’ claim on what remains.

Here is a worked example with a made-up shop owned by Ngozi. Every line balances.
Ngozi invests ₦500,000 cash: assets ₦500,000 = liabilities ₦0 + equity ₦500,000.
She borrows ₦200,000 from a bank: assets ₦700,000 = liabilities ₦200,000 + equity ₦500,000.
She buys equipment for ₦300,000 cash: assets stay at ₦700,000, with cash ₦400,000 and equipment ₦300,000.
She buys goods for ₦100,000 on credit: assets ₦800,000 = liabilities ₦300,000 + equity ₦500,000.
She sells half the goods, which cost ₦50,000, for ₦80,000 cash: assets ₦830,000 = liabilities ₦300,000 + equity ₦530,000. The ₦30,000 profit raises equity.

sections.heading: Double entry
sections.text: Each transaction has two sides. A debit increases an asset or an expense. A credit increases a liability, equity or income. When Ngozi buys equipment for cash, she debits equipment and credits cash. Total debits must equal total credits. A trial balance tests this, but it cannot catch every error. A transaction left out completely, for example, will not disturb the balance.

sections.heading: Accruals and depreciation
sections.text:
Under the accruals basis, income and expenses are recorded when they are earned or incurred, not when cash moves. Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. Under the straight-line method, the charge is (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. A van that costs R120,000, with a residual value of R20,000 and a five-year life, gives R20,000 a year.

Listed companies in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa generally report under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). The USA uses US GAAP. Rules change, so check the current official standard.

keyPoints: Assets = liabilities + equity, and this must hold after every transaction.
A debit increases assets and expenses.
A credit increases liabilities, equity and income.
Accruals accounting records items when earned or incurred, not when cash moves.
Straight-line depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life.
A balanced trial balance does not prove that the records are free of errors.

en.title: Financial Statements and Ratio Analysis
en.short: How to read the three main statements and calculate profitability, liquidity and gearing ratios.

sections.heading: The three main statements
sections.text:
The income statement, or profit and loss account, shows performance over a period. The statement of financial position, or balance sheet, shows assets, liabilities and equity at one date. The statement of cash flows shows cash from operating, investing and financing activities.

Profit and cash are different. A firm can report a profit and still run out of cash, because customers have not yet paid. Under IFRS, IAS 1 has governed presentation. IFRS 18 replaces it for periods starting on or after 1 January 2027, and it changes how the income statement is arranged. Check the rules that apply in your country.

sections.heading: A worked income statement
sections.text:
These figures for a made-up Ghanaian firm use an invented tax rate of 30%.
Revenue: GH₵900,000
Cost of sales: GH₵540,000
Gross profit: GH₵360,000
Operating expenses: GH₵210,000
Operating profit: GH₵150,000
Interest: GH₵30,000
Profit before tax: GH₵120,000
Tax at 30%: GH₵36,000
Profit after tax: GH₵84,000

sections.heading: Ratios from these figures
sections.text:
Suppose the firm also has current assets of GH₵300,000, including inventory of GH₵120,000. Its current liabilities are GH₵150,000, its long-term debt is GH₵200,000 and its equity is GH₵420,000.
Gross margin: 360,000 ÷ 900,000 = 40%
Net margin: 84,000 ÷ 900,000 = 9.3%
Return on equity: 84,000 ÷ 420,000 = 20%
Current ratio: 300,000 ÷ 150,000 = 2.0
Quick ratio: (300,000 − 120,000) ÷ 150,000 = 1.2
Gearing: 200,000 ÷ (200,000 + 420,000) = 32.3%
Interest cover: 150,000 ÷ 30,000 = 5 times

sections.heading: Using ratios well
sections.text: A ratio means little alone. Compare it with earlier years and with similar firms. A current ratio of 2.0 may be comfortable in one industry and wasteful in another. Definitions also vary, especially for gearing, so state the formula you use. Ask why a ratio has changed. Then look behind the numbers at accounting policies and one-off items.

keyPoints: The income statement covers a period, and the balance sheet shows one date.
Profit and cash are different, and a profitable firm can still run out of cash.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities.
The quick ratio leaves out inventory.
Compare ratios over time and with similar firms.
Gearing has several definitions, so state which one you use.

en.title: Business Statistics: Describing Data and Probability
en.short: Types of data, averages, standard deviation, basic probability and expected value for business decisions.

sections.heading: Types of data
sections.text: Statistics turns data into information for decisions. A population is the whole group of interest. A sample is the part you actually measure. Data can be qualitative, such as a region, or quantitative, such as sales. Levels of measurement are nominal (categories), ordinal (ordered categories), interval and ratio. Ratio data has a true zero, so a price of ₦200 is twice a price of ₦100.

sections.heading: Centre and spread
sections.text:
The mean is the sum of the values divided by their number. The median is the middle value when the values are in order. The mode is the most frequent value. A few extreme values pull the mean, so salaries are often better described by the median.

Spread shows how far values differ. Take a made-up kiosk’s weekly sales in thousands of shillings: 12, 15, 11, 18 and 14.
Mean: 70 ÷ 5 = 14
Deviations from the mean: −2, 1, −3, 4, 0
Squared deviations: 4, 1, 9, 16, 0, which sum to 30
Sample variance: 30 ÷ (5 − 1) = 7.5
Standard deviation: √7.5 = 2.74
The coefficient of variation is 2.74 ÷ 14 = 19.6%. It lets you compare spread between data sets of different sizes. Note that a sample variance divides by n − 1, while a population variance divides by n.

sections.heading: Probability and expected value
sections.text:
A probability lies between 0 and 1. If two events cannot happen together, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). If two events are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Expected value weights each outcome by its probability. Suppose a made-up project has a 0.6 chance of earning a profit of ₦500,000 and a 0.4 chance of losing ₦200,000.
Expected value = 0.6 × 500,000 + 0.4 × (−200,000) = 300,000 − 80,000 = ₦220,000
This is an average over many similar decisions. A small firm may reject the project anyway, because it cannot survive the loss.

keyPoints: A sample is the part of a population that you measure.
The median resists extreme values better than the mean.
Sample variance divides by n − 1.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance.
Expected value is a weighted average, not a guaranteed result.

en.title: Entrepreneurship and Small Business
en.short: Finding opportunities, testing business models, funding a start-up and understanding dilution and runway.

sections.heading: Opportunity and innovation
sections.text:
An entrepreneur spots an opportunity and organises resources to pursue it while accepting risk. Joseph Schumpeter described innovation as a force that replaces older firms and methods, which he called creative destruction. Many small businesses do not aim for this, and they provide steady local income and jobs. Definitions of a small or medium enterprise (SME) differ by country, so check the local one.

Two tools help to shape an idea. A business plan sets out the market, operations, team and finances. The Business Model Canvas, from Alexander Osterwalder, shows on one page how a firm creates, delivers and captures value. The lean start-up approach, made popular by Eric Ries, tests a simple version of the product with real customers, then learns and adjusts.

sections.heading: Funding and its arithmetic
sections.text:
Funding often begins with bootstrapping, which means using personal savings and early sales. Other sources include family, microfinance, banks, grants, angel investors and venture capital. Government agencies such as SMEDAN in Nigeria and the Ghana Enterprises Agency offer support to small firms. Loans must be repaid. Equity investors take a share of ownership.

A made-up start-up has ₦3,000,000 in cash and spends ₦250,000 more than it earns each month. This is its burn rate. Its runway is 3,000,000 ÷ 250,000 = 12 months.

Next, a made-up firm is valued at $800,000 before new money. An investor adds $200,000. The value after investment is $1,000,000. The investor owns 200,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 20%, and the founders fall from 100% to 80%. This reduction is called dilution.

sections.heading: A real example
sections.text: Paystack is a payments company founded in Lagos in 2015 by Shola Akinlade and Ezra Olubi. It helps businesses receive online payments. In October 2020, the US company Stripe agreed to buy it. The price was not officially published, but reports put it at more than US$200 million. One success does not show the typical result, and many new firms fail.

keyPoints: Entrepreneurs organise resources to pursue an opportunity under risk.
Lean start-up thinking tests ideas with real customers early.
Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn rate.
Investor’s share = investment ÷ value after investment.
Equity brings no repayment duty, but it dilutes the founders’ ownership.
SME definitions differ by country.

en.title: Human Resource Management
en.short: Planning, hiring, training, appraising and rewarding staff, with employment law by country.

sections.heading: The HR cycle
sections.text:
Human resource management (HRM) is the planned management of people at work. It starts with workforce planning, which compares the staff a firm will need with the staff it will have. Job analysis then records what a job involves. It produces a job description, which covers duties, and a person specification, which covers the skills required.

Recruitment attracts applicants, and selection chooses among them. Structured interviews and work samples tend to predict performance better than informal chats. Induction helps new staff to settle in.

sections.heading: Developing and rewarding people
sections.text:
Training builds skills for the present job, and development prepares people for future roles. Donald Kirkpatrick’s model evaluates training at four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

Performance appraisal reviews work against agreed goals. A 360-degree review collects views from managers, colleagues and others. Common errors include the halo effect, where one good quality colours the whole rating. Reward includes pay, benefits and non-financial rewards such as recognition. Internal fairness and fairness compared with the market both matter.

HR managers track measures such as labour turnover. A made-up Kampala hotel has 15 leavers in a year and an average of 120 staff.
Turnover = 15 ÷ 120 × 100 = 12.5%
Whether this is high depends on the industry and on which staff are leaving.

sections.heading: Employment law and relations
sections.text:
Employee relations covers contact between managers, staff and trade unions, including collective bargaining. Employment law differs by country. Examples are the Labour Act in Nigeria, the Labour Act 2003 (Act 651) in Ghana and the Employment Act 2007 in Kenya. South Africa has the Labour Relations Act 1995, the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 1997 and the Employment Equity Act 1998. The UK has the Employment Rights Act 1996 and the Equality Act 2010.

These laws commonly cover contracts, working hours, leave, dismissal and unfair discrimination. Details change, so check the current official source. This summary is for learning and is not legal advice.

keyPoints: HRM links workforce planning, hiring, development, reward and relations.
Job analysis produces a job description and a person specification.
Structured interviews usually predict performance better than informal ones.
Kirkpatrick’s levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results.
Labour turnover = leavers ÷ average staff × 100.
Employment law differs by country, so check the local statute.

en.title: Marketing Strategy, Pricing and Digital Marketing
en.short: Brands, pricing methods, price elasticity, mark-up against margin, and digital marketing measures.

sections.heading: Brands and adoption
sections.text:
A brand is the set of names, signs and beliefs that distinguish a product in the minds of buyers. Marketing communication aims to build awareness and preference, through advertising, public relations, sales promotion, personal selling and direct or digital contact.

Everett Rogers’s diffusion of innovation theory says that new products spread through groups. These are innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and laggards.

sections.heading: Pricing
sections.text:
Cost-based pricing adds a mark-up to cost. Value-based pricing starts from what the buyer will pay. Competition-based pricing follows rivals. Skimming starts high and falls later, while penetration starts low to win share quickly.

Mark-up and margin are different. A made-up item costs ₦800 and is priced with a 25% mark-up.
Price = 800 × 1.25 = ₦1,000
Profit = 1,000 − 800 = ₦200
Mark-up on cost = 200 ÷ 800 = 25%
Margin on price = 200 ÷ 1,000 = 20%

Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how buyers respond to a price change. PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price. A made-up shop raises a price from GH₵20 to GH₵22, which is a rise of 10%. Weekly sales fall from 1,000 to 950, which is a fall of 5%.
PED = −5% ÷ 10% = −0.5
Demand is inelastic, because the size of the result is below 1. Revenue rises from GH₵20,000 to 22 × 950 = GH₵20,900.

sections.heading: Digital marketing
sections.text:
Digital channels include search, social media, email and mobile messaging. They produce detailed data, which supports testing and targeting.

A made-up online shop in Cape Town spends R40,000 on advertising in a month. It gets 20,000 visits and 400 sales.
Conversion rate = 400 ÷ 20,000 = 2%
Customer acquisition cost = 40,000 ÷ 400 = R100
This spending is worthwhile only if the profit from a customer over time is greater than R100. Choose measures that link to the goal, not measures such as likes.

keyPoints: Mark-up is profit ÷ cost, and margin is profit ÷ price.
PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.
When demand is inelastic, a price rise increases revenue.
Skimming starts high, and penetration starts low.
Customer acquisition cost = marketing spend ÷ new customers.
Choose digital measures that link to the business goal.

en.title: Management Accounting: Costs, Break-even and Budgets
en.short: Cost behaviour, contribution, break-even, budgets and variances for internal decisions.

sections.heading: Purpose and costs
sections.text:
Management accounting gives managers information for planning and control. Unlike financial accounting, it is not usually governed by external reporting standards, and it can look to the future.

Fixed costs, such as rent, do not change with output in the short term. Variable costs, such as materials, change with output. Direct costs can be traced to a product, while indirect costs, called overheads, must be shared out. A sunk cost has already been spent and should not affect a future decision.

sections.heading: Cost-volume-profit analysis
sections.text:
Contribution is selling price minus variable cost. It first covers fixed costs and then adds to profit. A made-up Lagos workshop sells a chair for ₦2,000. The variable cost is ₦1,200, and fixed costs are ₦600,000 a year.
Contribution per chair = 2,000 − 1,200 = ₦800
Break-even units = 600,000 ÷ 800 = 750 chairs
Break-even revenue = 750 × 2,000 = ₦1,500,000
Units for a profit of ₦200,000 = (600,000 + 200,000) ÷ 800 = 1,000 chairs
Check: 1,000 × 800 − 600,000 = ₦200,000
Margin of safety at 1,000 chairs = (1,000 − 750) ÷ 1,000 = 25%
This model assumes a constant price and constant unit costs, which holds only within a limited range of output.

sections.heading: Budgets and variances
sections.text:
A budget is a financial plan for a period. A variance is the gap between budget or standard and the actual result. It is favourable when it raises profit and adverse when it lowers profit.

A made-up Pretoria firm makes 500 units. The standard is 2 kg per unit at R20 per kg. It actually uses 1,050 kg at R21 per kg.
Price variance = (21 − 20) × 1,050 = R1,050 adverse
Usage variance = (1,050 − 1,000) × 20 = R1,000 adverse
Total = 22,050 − 20,000 = R2,050 adverse
A variance only shows where to ask questions. Cheaper material, for example, can produce a favourable price variance and more waste.

keyPoints: Contribution = selling price − variable cost.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.
Sunk costs should not affect future decisions.
Adverse variances lower profit, and favourable variances raise it.
The price variance and the usage variance together explain the total material variance.
Break-even results hold only within a limited range of output.

en.title: Corporate Finance: Time Value and Investment Appraisal
en.short: Time value of money, with payback, net present value and internal rate of return worked through.

sections.heading: Time value of money
sections.text:
Corporate finance studies how firms choose investments and pay for them. Its first idea is that money today is worth more than the same amount later. It can be invested, inflation can reduce its buying power, and later payment carries risk.

Compounding moves money forward: future value = present value × (1 + r)ⁿ, where r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods. Discounting moves money back: present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. At 10%, KSh 100 grows to KSh 121 in two years. So KSh 121 due in two years has a present value of KSh 100.

sections.heading: A worked project
sections.text:
A made-up Mombasa firm can invest KSh 1,000,000 now. The project will return KSh 500,000 at the end of each of the next three years. Its required return is 10%.
Year 1: 500,000 ÷ 1.1 = 454,545
Year 2: 500,000 ÷ 1.21 = 413,223
Year 3: 500,000 ÷ 1.331 = 375,657
Total present value = 1,243,425 (1,243,426 before rounding each year)
NPV = 1,243,426 − 1,000,000 = KSh 243,426
The net present value (NPV) is positive, so the project adds value at this required return.
Payback = 1,000,000 ÷ 500,000 = 2 years
The internal rate of return (IRR) is the rate that makes NPV zero. Here it is about 23.4%, which is above the 10% required.

sections.heading: Comparing the methods
sections.text:
Payback is simple and shows how quickly cash returns. It ignores the time value of money and any cash after the payback date. IRR is easy to explain, but it can mislead when two projects compete.

NPV measures the expected change in value directly, so most finance textbooks prefer it. Use cash flows and not accounting profit. Include only future cash flows that change because of the decision, and leave out sunk costs. The result is only as good as the forecast, so test it with sensitivity analysis, which changes one assumption at a time.

keyPoints: Money today is worth more than the same amount later.
Present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.
Accept a project if NPV is positive, other things being equal.
IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero.
Payback ignores cash flows after the payback date.
Use future cash flows caused by the decision, and leave out sunk costs.

en.title: Corporate Finance: Funding, Cost of Capital and Working Capital
en.short: Debt and equity, CAPM, WACC, dividend valuation and managing the cash conversion cycle.

sections.heading: Debt, equity and capital structure
sections.text:
Firms raise long-term funds through debt, such as loans and bonds, and through equity, such as shares and retained profit. Debt requires interest and repayment, which raises financial risk. Interest is usually tax-deductible, however. Equity has no fixed payment, but shareholders expect a higher return because they carry more risk.

Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller showed in 1958 that, under strict assumptions, capital structure does not change firm value. The pecking order theory, from Stewart Myers and Nicholas Majluf, says firms prefer internal funds, then debt, then new equity.

sections.heading: Finding required returns
sections.text:
The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) estimates the return on equity: Re = Rf + β(Rm − Rf). Here Rf is the risk-free rate, Rm is the market return, and β measures how strongly a share moves with the market. With Rf = 5%, Rm = 11% and β = 1.2:
Re = 5% + 1.2 × 6% = 12.2%

The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) combines both funding types. A made-up firm in Leeds has 60% equity at 18%, and 40% debt at 15% before tax. The invented tax rate is 30%.
WACC = 0.6 × 18% + 0.4 × 15% × (1 − 0.3) = 10.8% + 4.2% = 15%

The dividend growth model values a share: P = D₁ ÷ (r − g). Here D₁ is next year’s dividend, r is the required return and g is constant growth. With D₁ = ₦2, r = 12% and g = 4%:
P = 2 ÷ 0.08 = ₦25

sections.heading: Working capital
sections.text: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Too little can stop a firm paying its bills, and too much ties up cash. The cash conversion cycle measures how long cash stays tied up in operations. It equals inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. A firm with 45, 30 and 35 days has a cycle of 45 + 30 − 35 = 40 days.

keyPoints: Debt is usually cheaper than equity, but it adds financial risk.
CAPM: Re = Rf + β(Rm − Rf).
WACC weights each funding source and uses after-tax debt cost.
The dividend growth model needs r to be greater than g.
Cash conversion cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.

en.title: Operations Management: Processes, Capacity and Quality
en.short: Turning inputs into outputs: process types, capacity, productivity, quality and lean methods.

sections.heading: Transforming inputs
sections.text: Operations management designs and runs the process that turns inputs, such as materials and labour, into goods and services. Process types range from project work through job and batch production to mass production and continuous flow. As volume rises, variety usually falls and unit cost falls too. Services differ from goods, because customers often take part, and an empty hotel room tonight cannot be stored for tomorrow.

sections.heading: Capacity and productivity
sections.text:
Capacity is the maximum output in a period. Utilisation is actual output divided by capacity. A bottleneck is the slowest stage, and it limits the whole process. Eliyahu Goldratt’s theory of constraints focuses improvement there.

A made-up Kumasi garment workshop has 8 workers on an 8-hour day. It makes 400 shirts a day, and its capacity is 500 a day.
Labour hours = 8 × 8 = 64
Labour productivity = 400 ÷ 64 = 6.25 shirts per hour
Utilisation = 400 ÷ 500 = 80%
Full utilisation is not always a good aim, because queues grow quickly as a process nears its limit.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.text: Quality means meeting customer requirements consistently. Total quality management (TQM) makes quality the duty of everyone. W. Edwards Deming promoted the plan, do, check, act cycle. Statistical process control uses control charts to separate normal variation from special causes. Six Sigma, developed at Motorola, aims to reduce variation. Its often-quoted target is 3.4 defects per million opportunities.

sections.heading: Lean thinking
sections.text: Lean methods aim to remove waste, which is any activity that adds no value for the customer. They grew from the Toyota Production System in Japan, which rests on two main ideas. Just-in-time makes only what is needed, when it is needed. Jidoka lets a machine or worker stop the line when a problem appears, so that defects do not move on. Taiichi Ohno of Toyota played a leading part in developing the system. Just-in-time requires reliable suppliers. Where transport or power supply is uncertain, firms may reasonably hold more stock.

keyPoints: As volume rises, variety and unit cost usually fall.
Productivity = output ÷ input, and utilisation = actual output ÷ capacity.
A bottleneck limits the output of the whole process.
The Deming cycle is plan, do, check, act.
Lean aims to remove activity that adds no value for the customer.
The Toyota system rests on just-in-time and jidoka.

en.title: Supply Chain and Inventory Management
en.short: Linking suppliers to customers, EOQ, reorder points, the bullwhip effect and a drone delivery case.

sections.heading: The chain
sections.text:
A supply chain is the network of firms and activities that moves a product from raw material to final customer. Supply chain management coordinates flows of goods, money and information across that network. Procurement buys inputs. Logistics stores and moves goods.

Small changes in customer demand can grow as orders pass up the chain, because each stage adds its own forecast and safety margin. This is the bullwhip effect. Sharing sales data across firms can reduce it.

Ghana offers a real example of logistics design. In April 2019, Zipline began using drones in Ghana to deliver medical products to health facilities, starting from a centre at Omenako in the Eastern Region.

sections.heading: How much to order
sections.text:
Inventory is stock held for later use. Holding too much ties up cash and risks waste. Holding too little loses sales.

The economic order quantity (EOQ) balances ordering cost and holding cost: EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H). D is annual demand, S is the cost per order and H is the holding cost per unit per year.

A made-up Abuja distributor sells 10,000 units a year. Each order costs ₦5,000, and holding a unit costs ₦400 a year.
EOQ = √(2 × 10,000 × 5,000 ÷ 400) = √250,000 = 500 units
Orders per year = 10,000 ÷ 500 = 20
Annual ordering cost = 20 × 5,000 = ₦100,000
Annual holding cost = (500 ÷ 2) × 400 = ₦100,000
The two costs are equal at the EOQ, which is a useful check.

sections.heading: When to order
sections.text:
The reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order. It equals demand during the lead time plus any safety stock. The lead time is the wait between ordering and delivery. Suppose daily demand is 40 units, lead time is 5 days and safety stock is 50 units.
Reorder point = 40 × 5 + 50 = 250 units
The EOQ assumes steady demand, so firms adjust safety stock when supply is uncertain.

keyPoints: Supply chains carry goods, money and information.
The bullwhip effect makes demand swings larger further up the chain.
EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H).
At the EOQ, annual ordering cost equals annual holding cost.
Reorder point = lead-time demand + safety stock.

en.title: Business Law: Contracts, Companies and Agency
en.short: Contract formation, separate corporate personality, agency and consumer protection across countries.

sections.heading: Contracts
sections.text:
A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. Common law systems, including those of Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and England, generally require offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations and capacity. Consideration means that each side gives something of value. South African law, with Roman-Dutch roots, differs here, because it does not require consideration.

An offer is different from an invitation to treat. A price display in a shop is usually an invitation, so the customer makes the offer. In Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256 (England), a firm promised money to anyone who used its product and still caught influenza. The court held that this was an offer to the whole world, accepted by those who did what it asked. The usual remedy for breach is damages.

sections.heading: Companies
sections.text: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members. Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22 (House of Lords, UK) is the classic authority. Courts may look behind the company in limited cases, such as fraud. This is called lifting or piercing the corporate veil. The main statutes include the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (Nigeria), the Companies Act 2019, Act 992 (Ghana), the Companies Act 2015 (Kenya), the Companies Act 71 of 2008 (South Africa) and the Companies Act 2006 (UK). Directors generally owe duties to the company, such as acting in good faith and avoiding conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Agency and consumers
sections.text:
An agent acts for a principal and can bind the principal to contracts with third parties.

Consumer law limits unfair dealing. Examples are Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018, Kenya’s Consumer Protection Act 2012, South Africa’s Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 and the UK’s Consumer Rights Act 2015.

Law changes and differs by country. This summary is for learning and is not legal advice. Check the current official source.

keyPoints: Common law contracts generally need offer, acceptance, consideration, intention and capacity.
South African contract law does not require consideration.
A shop display is usually an invitation to treat, not an offer.
Salomon is the classic authority for separate corporate personality.
Courts lift the corporate veil only in limited cases.
An agent can bind a principal to contracts with third parties.

en.title: Business Ethics and Corporate Governance
en.short: Ethical theories, agency problems, boards, audit, CSR and lessons from Enron and Steinhoff.

sections.heading: Ethical thinking
sections.text:
Business ethics asks what is right in business, beyond what the law requires. Utilitarianism judges an act by its results for all affected people. Deontology, linked with Immanuel Kant, judges an act by duties and rules. Virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do. African thought adds ubuntu, which stresses shared humanity and duty to the community.

Milton Friedman argued in 1970 that a firm’s social responsibility is to increase profit while staying within the rules. R. Edward Freeman’s stakeholder theory says managers should consider all groups affected by the firm. Archie Carroll’s pyramid of corporate social responsibility (CSR) has economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic layers. ESG reporting covers environmental, social and governance performance.

sections.heading: Corporate governance
sections.text:
Corporate governance is the system that directs and controls companies. Agency theory, from Michael Jensen and William Meckling, says that managers, as agents, may not always act in the interest of owners, who are the principals. Common controls include independent directors, audit committees, external audit, disclosure and pay linked to performance.

Countries approach this differently. Nigeria has a national code from its Financial Reporting Council, South Africa has the King reports, and the UK has its Corporate Governance Code. Anti-bribery laws include the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act 1977, the UK Bribery Act 2010 and Kenya’s Bribery Act 2016. Check the current version of any code or law.

sections.heading: Two real failures
sections.text:
Enron, a US energy company, filed for bankruptcy in December 2001 after an accounting scandal. The USA passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002, which tightened rules on audit and financial reporting.

In December 2017, the retail group Steinhoff, listed in Johannesburg and Frankfurt, announced accounting irregularities. A summary of a PwC investigation, released in 2019, said that fictitious or irregular transactions inflated profits and assets. It listed about €6.5 billion of such income from 2009 to 2017.

These cases show why independent checks matter, and why people need safe ways to report wrongdoing, called whistleblowing.

keyPoints: Utilitarianism looks at results, and deontology looks at duties.
Friedman stresses profit within the rules, and Freeman stresses all stakeholders.
Agency theory explains why owners need controls over managers.
Carroll’s pyramid is economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic.
Enron contributed to the US Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.
Governance codes differ by country.

en.title: Business Statistics: Inference and Regression
en.short: Sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and regression for business forecasting.

sections.heading: Sampling and confidence intervals
sections.text:
Inference uses a sample to draw conclusions about a population. Random samples allow the error to be estimated. Convenience samples may be biased.

The standard error is SE = s ÷ √n. A made-up survey of 100 Nairobi customers finds mean monthly spending of KSh 5,000, with a standard deviation of KSh 800.
SE = 800 ÷ √100 = 80
95% interval = 5,000 ± 1.96 × 80 = 5,000 ± 156.8
The interval runs from KSh 4,843.2 to KSh 5,156.8. In repeated sampling, about 95% of intervals made this way would contain the true mean. For small samples, use the t distribution in place of 1.96.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.text:
A test starts with a null hypothesis (H₀), which usually says there is no effect or no difference. Suppose last year’s mean was KSh 4,800, and H₀ says it has not changed.
Test statistic = (5,000 − 4,800) ÷ 80 = 2.5
At the 5% level in a two-sided test, the critical value is 1.96. Because 2.5 is greater than 1.96, we reject H₀.

The p-value is the probability of a result at least this extreme if H₀ is true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true. A Type I error rejects a true H₀. A Type II error fails to reject a false H₀. A statistically significant result may still be too small to matter in practice. Other common tests are t-tests, chi-square and ANOVA.

sections.heading: Correlation and regression
sections.text:
The correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to +1 and measures the strength of a straight-line relationship. Regression fits an equation that predicts one variable from others. Suppose a made-up firm in Soweto estimates weekly sales = 20 + 3x, where x is advertising spending in thousands of rand. If x = 10, predicted sales are 20 + 3 × 10 = 50 units.

Correlation does not prove causation. A hidden factor, such as a holiday season, may increase both advertising and sales.

keyPoints: Standard error = s ÷ √n.
A 95% interval for a mean, in large samples, is mean ± 1.96 × SE.
The p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true.
Type I rejects a true H₀, and Type II fails to reject a false H₀.
Statistical significance does not always mean practical importance.
Correlation does not prove causation.

en.title: Strategic Management
en.short: Analysing industries and resources, choosing a competitive strategy and measuring its results.

sections.heading: What strategy is
sections.text: Strategy is the set of long-term choices that decide where a firm competes and how it wins. Competitive advantage means performing better than rivals in a way that lasts. Henry Mintzberg separates deliberate strategy, which is planned, from emergent strategy, which forms from actions over time.

sections.heading: External and internal analysis
sections.text:
Michael Porter’s five forces describe the pressures on industry profit: rivalry among competitors, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, the bargaining power of buyers and the bargaining power of suppliers.

Internal analysis looks inside the firm. Porter’s value chain breaks a firm into primary and support activities, to show where value and cost arise. The resource-based view, linked with Jay Barney, says that lasting advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and well organised. This is the VRIO test. C. K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel wrote about core competences, which are collective skills that competitors find hard to copy. SWOT brings the results together as strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. A SWOT list has little value unless it leads to choices.

sections.heading: Competitive strategy
sections.text:
Porter named three generic strategies. Cost leadership aims to be the lowest-cost producer in an industry. Differentiation offers something buyers value and will pay more for. Focus serves a narrow segment, using either low cost or differentiation.

Capitec Bank in South Africa, founded in 2001, is often discussed in this context. It built its model around simple retail banking, offering one main account in place of many premium tiers. By 2025 it was reported as the country’s largest retail bank by number of customers. Students should debate which label fits it best, because real firms rarely fit one category.

sections.heading: Putting it into action
sections.text: Good plans fail when structure, staff and budgets do not support them. Robert Kaplan and David Norton’s balanced scorecard measures four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth. It stops managers from looking only at short-term profit.

keyPoints: Strategy is about where to compete and how to win.
The five forces explain the pressures on industry profit.
VRIO tests whether a resource can give lasting advantage.
Porter’s generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus.
SWOT must lead to choices, or it has little value.
The balanced scorecard has four perspectives.

en.title: International Business
en.short: Why firms go abroad, how they enter markets, trade blocs, culture and exchange rate risk.

sections.heading: Why firms cross borders
sections.text:
International business covers trade and investment across national borders. David Ricardo’s theory of comparative advantage says countries gain when each specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost. Firms go abroad to find markets, resources, lower costs or new skills. Foreign direct investment (FDI) means owning and controlling operations abroad. John Dunning’s eclectic paradigm explains it through ownership, location and internalisation advantages.

Trade blocs reduce barriers among members. Examples are ECOWAS, the East African Community, SADC and the EU. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) entered into force in May 2019, and trading under it formally began on 1 January 2021. Its secretariat is in Accra.

sections.heading: Entry modes and real cases
sections.text:
Entry modes differ in cost, control and risk. They include exporting, licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries. The Uppsala model, from Jan Johanson and Jan-Erik Vahlne, says many firms expand step by step as they learn.

Three real cases show the range. Blue Skies, founded in Ghana in the late 1990s, cuts and packs fresh fruit near where it grows and sends it to European retailers, so more value stays close to the source. MTN of South Africa paid US$285 million in 2001 for one of Nigeria’s mobile licences. Shoprite of South Africa sold its Nigerian business in 2021 to Ketron Investment. Reports at the time named supply problems and difficulty in moving funds out of the country.

sections.heading: Culture and currency risk
sections.text:
Geert Hofstede compared national cultures on dimensions such as power distance and individualism. These are broad averages and should not be used to stereotype individuals.

Exchange rates create risk. A made-up Ghanaian importer owes £10,000 in three months. The invented rate today is £1 = GH₵15, which gives a cost of GH₵150,000. If the rate moves to £1 = GH₵16.5, the cost is GH₵165,000. That is GH₵15,000 or 10% more. A forward contract, which fixes a rate today for a later date, can reduce this risk.

keyPoints: Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost.
FDI means owning and controlling operations abroad.
Entry modes trade off cost, control and risk.
Regional blocs include ECOWAS, EAC, SADC and AfCFTA.
National culture scores are averages, not descriptions of individuals.
A forward contract fixes an exchange rate today for a later date.

en.title: Management Information Systems
en.short: Types of information systems, ERP and CRM, data analytics, security and data protection law.

sections.heading: Systems for each level
sections.text:
An information system collects, stores and shares information to support decisions and operations. Data are raw facts, and information is data given meaning.

Transaction processing systems record daily events, such as sales. Management information systems summarise these into regular reports. Decision support systems help managers to test options. An enterprise resource planning (ERP) system joins functions such as finance, stock and HR around one database. Customer relationship management (CRM) systems store customer contact and sales history. Business intelligence tools analyse data for patterns. Projects often fail because of poor processes, weak training or staff resistance, and not only because of the software. Fred Davis’s technology acceptance model says that use depends on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use.

sections.heading: Technology and business models
sections.text:
Information systems can also change what a business offers. In March 2007, Safaricom launched M-Pesa in Kenya, with support from Vodafone. It lets people send and store money using a mobile phone and a network of agents. It is a common case study in how a telecoms firm moved into financial services.

Cloud computing rents computing power and software over the internet. It can reduce upfront cost, but it adds reliance on the provider and on the network.

sections.heading: Evaluating and protecting systems
sections.text:
A made-up Johannesburg firm pays R500,000 for a new system, and it saves R200,000 a year.
Payback = 500,000 ÷ 200,000 = 2.5 years
A service promising 99.9% availability may be down for 0.1% of the time. Over a year, that is 365 × 24 × 0.001 = 8.76 hours.

Information security aims for confidentiality, integrity and availability. Phishing, stolen passwords and unpatched software are frequent weak points. Data protection laws set duties for handling personal data. They include the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, Ghana’s Data Protection Act 2012, Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019, South Africa’s Protection of Personal Information Act 2013 and the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation. Check the current official source for your country.

keyPoints: Information is data given meaning.
ERP systems join business functions around one database.
CRM systems store customer contact and sales history.
Security aims for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Data protection laws differ by country.
System projects often fail because of people and processes, not only software.

en.title: Corporate Strategy: Growth, Portfolios and Acquisitions
en.short: What businesses a group should own: diversification, integration, portfolios, mergers and synergy.

sections.heading: Direction of growth
sections.text:
Corporate strategy asks which businesses a group should own, and how the centre adds value to them. H. Igor Ansoff’s matrix sets out four growth paths: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification. Risk generally rises as a firm moves further from its current products and markets.

Vertical integration brings another stage of the supply chain inside the firm. Related diversification shares skills or assets across businesses, and unrelated diversification has fewer links.

Dangote Group of Nigeria illustrates these paths. It began in trading, moved from importing cement to making it, and later built a refinery at Lekki with a design capacity of 650,000 barrels a day.

sections.heading: Managing a portfolio
sections.text: The Boston Consulting Group’s growth-share matrix groups business units by market growth and relative market share. Stars have high growth and high share. Cash cows have low growth and high share, and they often fund others. Question marks have high growth and low share. Dogs have low growth and low share. The matrix is a simple starting point, and it ignores links between units. Michael Goold and Andrew Campbell ask a harder question: does this parent add more value to a unit than another owner would?

sections.heading: Acquisitions and synergy
sections.text:
An acquirer hopes for synergy, which means the combined firm is worth more than the two separate firms. Consider a made-up deal in millions of dollars.
Acquirer’s value: 500
Target’s value: 200
Combined value: 800
Synergy = 800 − 500 − 200 = 100
Cash price paid: 240, a premium of 40
Acquirer’s gain = 100 − 40 = 60
Check: 800 − 240 − 500 = 60

In October 2016, AB InBev completed its purchase of SABMiller, a brewer whose origins go back to South African Breweries, founded in 1895. The headline value was about £79 billion. Regulators required the sale of certain assets, which shows that competition law can shape a deal.

keyPoints: Corporate strategy decides which businesses to own and how the centre adds value.
Ansoff’s paths are penetration, market development, product development and diversification.
The BCG matrix uses market growth and relative share.
Synergy = combined value − the two separate values.
The acquirer gains only if synergy is greater than the premium.
Competition regulators can require asset sales as a condition of a deal.

en.title: Leadership and Organisational Change
en.short: Leadership theories from traits to transformation, and models for leading change and resistance.

sections.heading: Leadership theories
sections.text:
Leadership is the process of influencing people toward shared goals. Trait theories looked for qualities that leaders share, and the results were mixed. Behavioural studies at Ohio State and Michigan separated concern for tasks from concern for people.

Contingency theories argue that effectiveness depends on the situation. Fred Fiedler matched leader style to the favourability of the situation. Robert House’s path-goal theory says leaders should clear the way to goals. Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard linked style to the readiness of followers.

James MacGregor Burns and Bernard Bass separated transactional leadership, which exchanges rewards for performance, from transformational leadership, which inspires people to go beyond self-interest. Critics warn against treating leaders as heroes, because results also depend on followers, systems and luck. The GLOBE project studied how ideas of good leadership vary across cultures, so do not assume one model applies everywhere.

sections.heading: Models of change
sections.text: Kurt Lewin’s model is usually described as three steps: unfreeze, move and refreeze. John Kotter proposed eight steps: create urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a vision, communicate it, remove barriers, win short-term gains, build on them, and anchor the change in culture. Critics say that real change is messier, so emergent approaches treat it as ongoing learning. A common claim says that most change programmes fail, but the evidence for any exact figure is weak, so do not quote one without a source.

sections.heading: Resistance and a real warning
sections.text:
People resist change for reasons such as fear of job loss, loss of status, poor communication and distrust. Resistance can also contain useful information. Good responses include involving people early, honest communication and training.

At Eastman Kodak, an engineer, Steven Sasson, built an early digital camera in 1975. It led US digital camera sales in 2005, but it still filed for bankruptcy protection in the USA in January 2012. Writers still disagree about the main causes. Protecting an existing business is one common explanation, but market and technology changes also played a part.

keyPoints: Theories moved from traits to behaviours, then to contingency and transformation.
Transactional leaders exchange rewards, and transformational leaders inspire.
Contingency theories say effectiveness depends on the situation.
Lewin’s steps are unfreeze, move and refreeze.
Kotter’s model has eight steps, from urgency to culture.
Resistance can contain useful information, so listen to it.

en.title: Research Methods for Business
en.short: Designing a dissertation: philosophy, design, sampling, sample size, validity, analysis and ethics.

sections.heading: From question to design
sections.text:
A dissertation begins with a clear question that matters to the field. A literature review then shows what is known, compares sources critically and exposes a gap.

Positivism looks for measurable patterns and tests theory. Interpretivism seeks to understand the meanings people give to events. Pragmatism chooses whatever methods answer the question best. Deductive research tests existing theory, while inductive research builds theory from data.

Common designs are surveys, experiments, case studies, interviews and archival analysis. Quantitative work uses numbers, and qualitative work uses words and meanings. Mixed methods combine the two.

sections.heading: Sampling and sample size
sections.text:
Probability sampling, such as simple random or stratified sampling, supports statistical generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or snowball sampling, is common in qualitative work.

Students often use published formulas, so learn their assumptions. Yamane’s formula is n = N ÷ (1 + Ne²). With a population of 2,000 and a 5% margin of error:
n = 2,000 ÷ (1 + 2,000 × 0.05²) = 2,000 ÷ 6 = 333.3, so use 334
Cochran’s formula for a large population is n = z²pq ÷ e². With z = 1.96, p = q = 0.5 and e = 0.05:
n = 3.8416 × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 384.16, so use 385
Both assume random sampling and estimate a proportion. They do not correct for bias or low response rates.

sections.heading: Quality and analysis
sections.text:
Validity asks whether you measure what you intend to measure. Reliability asks whether the measure is consistent. Cronbach’s alpha is often used for scales, and a value of 0.7 is a common guide, though not a strict rule.

For numbers, choose tests that match the data and the question, such as regression or ANOVA. For text, thematic analysis, as set out by Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, is widely used.

sections.heading: Ethics
sections.text: Researchers need informed consent, and they must protect participants from harm and keep data confidential. Most universities require ethical approval before data collection. Cite every source, and never fabricate data.

keyPoints: A literature review compares sources and exposes a gap.
Deductive research tests theory, and inductive research builds it.
Choose the design that fits the question.
Yamane: n = N ÷ (1 + Ne²).
Sample size formulas do not correct for bias or low response.
Validity is about accuracy, and reliability is about consistency.
Informed consent and confidentiality are basic research duties.
